planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a shaded woodland setting; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun.

directions: Named for Dr. Richard Jaynes, the Connecticut plant breeder widely regarded as the foremost authority on Kalmia latifolia and author of the reference text Kalmia: Mountain Laurel and Related Species. North Carolina State Extension lists this selection as notably shade tolerant with heavy flowering, making it a reliable choice for darker woodland sites where many mountain laurel cultivars bloom more sparsely. Site in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath high canopy, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and soil acidity. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.
sources: Richard A. Jaynes, Kalmia: Mountain Laurel and Related Species (Timber Press, 1997)
